issues.legal_issue: Sustainable development is a principle of environmental law that reconciles development with environmental protection.
material_facts: The leather industry generated foreign exchange and employment, but tannery effluent had polluted water and land, damaged agriculture, and threatened residents’ health.
The Court considered the international development of sustainable development, including the Stockholm Declaration, the Brundtland Report, and the 1992 Rio Conference.
issues.conclusion: Sustainable development is a balancing concept between ecology and development and has been accepted as part of customary international law, although its salient features have not all been finalized.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the Brundtland Report’s definition of sustainable development as development that meets present needs without compromising future generations’ ability to meet their needs. It treated inter-generational equity, conservation of natural resources, environmental protection, and related principles as features of sustainable development, and identified the precautionary principle and polluter pays principle as essential features.

rule.if: environmental_public_interest_proceeding and (development_activity or economic_benefit) and environmental_harm_or_risk

predicates.environmental_public_interest_proceeding: The proceeding concerns public interests affected by environmental conditions.
predicates.development_activity: An activity is undertaken for development or economic purposes.
predicates.economic_benefit: The activity provides an economic benefit.
predicates.environmental_harm_or_risk: The activity has caused or may cause harm to the environment.

issues.definition: When an environmental public-interest proceeding concerns development or economic benefit alongside environmental harm or risk, the rule requires development to be balanced with environmental protection.

issues.legal_issue: The precautionary principle is part of domestic environmental law and places the burden on the actor or developer to show that its activity is environmentally benign.
material_facts: Tanneries discharged untreated or inadequately treated effluent, contaminating groundwater and rivers and damaging agricultural land.
Expert reports recorded that water near tannery clusters was unfit for drinking and that treatment plants were not consistently meeting required standards.
The Court held that threats of serious and irreversible environmental damage should not be left unaddressed merely because scientific certainty is lacking.
issues.conclusion: The precautionary principle is part of the law of the land; environmental measures must anticipate, prevent, and attack the causes of degradation, and the actor or developer bears the burden of showing its action is environmentally benign.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the precautionary principle as an essential feature of sustainable development and part of domestic environmental law. It relied on Article 21 and Articles 47, 48A, and 51A(g) of the Constitution, environmental legislation, and the principle’s status in customary international law. It also referred to Addl. District Magistrate, Jabalpur v. Shivakant Shukla (AIR 1976 SC 1207), Jolly George Varghese (AIR 1980 SC 470), and Gramophone Company (AIR 1984 SC 667) for the incorporation of customary international law into domestic law when it is not contrary to municipal law.

rule.if: environmental_public_interest_proceeding and environmental_harm_or_risk and (serious_or_irreversible_threat or scientific_uncertainty)

predicates.environmental_public_interest_proceeding: The proceeding concerns public interests affected by environmental conditions.
predicates.environmental_harm_or_risk: An activity has caused or may cause environmental harm.
predicates.serious_or_irreversible_threat: The threatened environmental damage is serious or irreversible.
predicates.scientific_uncertainty: Scientific certainty about the environmental threat or its effects is lacking.

issues.definition: In an environmental public-interest proceeding involving environmental harm or risk and a serious or irreversible threat or scientific uncertainty, the actor must take precautionary measures and show that its activity is environmentally benign.

issues.legal_issue: The polluter pays principle makes a polluting actor liable both to compensate affected persons and to pay the cost of restoring environmental damage, including damage caused in the past.
material_facts: Tannery effluent had polluted water and soil, impaired agricultural land, and caused hardship and health risks for residents.
The tanneries had operated and polluted the area for years, including some that had by then installed pollution-control equipment.
The Court directed assessment of compensation for affected persons and the cost of reversing environmental damage.
issues.conclusion: Polluting industries are absolutely liable to compensate affected persons and to pay the cost of restoring the damaged environment; liability for past pollution remains even if an industry has since installed pollution-control devices.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the polluter pays principle as an essential feature of sustainable development and part of domestic environmental law. It relied on Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India, J.T. 1996 (2) 196, which applied absolute liability to hazardous or inherently dangerous activities regardless of reasonable care. The Court also relied on Article 21 and Articles 47, 48A, and 51A(g) of the Constitution, environmental legislation, and the rule that customary international law forms part of domestic law when not contrary to municipal law.

predicates.environmental_public_interest_proceeding: The proceeding concerns public interests affected by environmental conditions.
predicates.polluting_activity: An actor’s activity releases pollutants into the environment.
predicates.environmental_or_personal_harm: The pollution has harmed the environment or people affected by it.

issues.definition: When a polluting activity causes environmental or personal harm in an environmental public-interest proceeding, the polluter must compensate victims and pay for environmental restoration.

issues.legal_issue: The right to a clean environment is protected as part of the right to life and is also grounded in constitutional provisions and common law.
material_facts: Effluent from tanneries contaminated surface and groundwater, including water used for drinking, and degraded land and the surrounding environment.
Residents faced acute shortages of drinking water, and expert reports found water near tannery clusters unfit for drinking.
The Court considered the constitutional provisions concerning life, public health, and environmental protection, as well as the common-law right to a clean environment.
issues.conclusion: The constitutional and statutory provisions protect a person’s right to fresh air, clean water, and a pollution-free environment, and the right is also an inalienable common-law right and part of the basic jurisprudence of the country.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on Article 21 and Articles 47, 48A, and 51A(g) of the Constitution, the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act 1974, the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act 1981, and the Environment (Protection) Act 1986. It also relied on the common-law principle against nuisance, illustrated by Blackstone’s Commentaries on the Laws of England.

predicates.environmental_public_interest_proceeding: The proceeding concerns public interests affected by environmental conditions.
predicates.pollution_threatens_health_or_life: Pollution threatens people’s health or life, including through contamination of essential resources.

issues.definition: When pollution threatens health or life in an environmental public-interest proceeding, the right to a clean environment is protected.

issues.legal_issue: The Central Government must constitute an empowered authority when statutory environmental powers need to be exercised to address persistent pollution.
material_facts: The Environment (Protection) Act 1986 empowered the Central Government to take measures to protect and improve the environment and to create an authority under section 3(3) with relevant powers.
No such authority had been constituted, despite serious and persistent pollution by tanneries and other industries.
The Court considered that the authority was needed to assess harm, compensation, and restoration and to exercise powers including issuing directions under section 5.
issues.conclusion: The Central Government was directed to constitute an authority under section 3(3) of the Environment (Protection) Act 1986, confer the necessary powers on it, and assign it responsibility for addressing the pollution situation.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3(3) of the Environment (Protection) Act 1986 empowers the Central Government to constitute an authority and confer specified powers and functions on it. Section 5 authorizes written directions, including directions for closure, prohibition, or regulation of an industry. The Court held that the Act’s pollution-control and environmental-protection purposes required an empowered authority to be established in the circumstances.

predicates.environmental_public_interest_proceeding: The proceeding concerns public interests affected by environmental conditions.
predicates.persistent_environmental_pollution: Pollution has continued despite efforts or opportunities to control it.
predicates.environmental_authority_not_constituted: The government has not constituted an authority needed to exercise environmental-protection powers.

issues.definition: When persistent environmental pollution is addressed in an environmental public-interest proceeding and the necessary authority has not been constituted, the Central Government must constitute and empower that authority.

issues.legal_issue: Pollution-control standards set by a State Pollution Control Board may be stricter than general standards and must be complied with when supported by expert assessment.
material_facts: Tanneries challenged the Board’s standard for total dissolved solids in discharges.
The Environment (Protection) Rules permitted a Board to specify more stringent standards for a particular industry based on the recipient system and recorded reasons.
NEERI examined the standard and justified it on environmental, health, and practical grounds; it also reported that the standard could be met with proper process controls and treatment plants.
issues.conclusion: The Board’s standards for total dissolved solids, as supported by NEERI, were to remain operative and be complied with by tanneries and other industries in the State.
issues.legal_principle: Rule 3(2) of the Environment (Protection) Rules 1986 permits a Pollution Control Board to specify more stringent standards than those generally provided, depending on the quality of the recipient system and after recording reasons. Sections 7 and 3 of the Environment (Protection) Act 1986 concern discharge standards and environmental-protection measures. The Court relied on NEERI’s expert assessment of the standards.

predicates.environmental_public_interest_proceeding: The proceeding concerns public interests affected by environmental conditions.
predicates.board_sets_discharge_standard: A pollution-control board has set a standard for discharges from an industry or process.
predicates.expert_assessment_supports_standard: An expert assessment supports the standard on environmental or health grounds.

issues.definition: When a board sets a discharge standard in an environmental public-interest proceeding and expert assessment supports it, industries must comply with that standard.

issues.legal_issue: Industries causing pollution may be required to install effective pollution-control devices and obtain operating consent, and may be closed if they fail to do so.
material_facts: Many tanneries had failed over several years, despite repeated opportunities and notices, to establish satisfactory individual treatment plants or connect to common treatment plants.
Reports showed that treatment plants were not consistently operating satisfactorily and that water near tannery clusters was unfit for drinking.
The Court directed the tanneries to install individual or common pollution-control systems, obtain the Board’s consent to operate, and face closure if they failed to obtain consent.
issues.conclusion: The tanneries were required to install the necessary pollution-control devices and obtain the Board’s consent to operate; those that failed to obtain consent were to be closed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act 1974, which restricts the use of streams and wells for polluting discharges and requires consent for outlets and effluent discharges, and on sections 5 and 7 of the Environment (Protection) Act 1986, which permit directions including closure and prohibit discharges exceeding prescribed standards. The Court also relied on its prior orders in the proceeding and expert reports documenting inadequate treatment and pollution.

predicates.environmental_public_interest_proceeding: The proceeding concerns public interests affected by environmental conditions.
predicates.industrial_pollution: An industrial activity is causing or contributing to pollution.
predicates.pollution_controls_inadequate: The industry’s pollution-control equipment or treatment arrangements are absent or do not adequately control its discharges.

issues.definition: When industrial pollution continues and controls are inadequate in an environmental public-interest proceeding, the industry must install effective controls and obtain operating consent or be closed.

issues.legal_issue: A ban on locating highly polluting industries within a specified area around protected water sources must be enforced, and existing industries in that area may be reviewed for relocation.
material_facts: A government order prohibited specified highly polluting industries from being set up within one kilometre of designated water sources.
Tanneries were listed as highly polluting industries under that order.

The Court expressed doubt that the order was being enforced and directed that it be enforced forthwith and that existing industries in the prohibited area be reviewed, with relocation available as an option.
issues.conclusion: The government order was to be enforced, no new listed industry was to be permitted in the prohibited area, and the authority could review existing industries and direct relocation.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Government Order No. 213 of March 30, 1989, which imposed a ban on locating listed highly polluting industries within one kilometre of specified water sources. It also relied on the Environment (Protection) Act 1986, including the Central Government’s powers to restrict areas for industrial activity and issue directions concerning industry closure, prohibition, or regulation.

predicates.environmental_public_interest_proceeding: The proceeding concerns public interests affected by environmental conditions.
predicates.highly_polluting_industry: The proposed activity belongs to a class of industries identified as highly polluting.
predicates.proposed_location_within_protected_water: The proposed site is within a protected distance of a designated water source.

issues.definition: When a highly polluting industry is proposed within a protected water zone in an environmental public-interest proceeding, the new industry must not be permitted there.

issues.legal_issue: The High Court was the appropriate forum to continue monitoring the environmental matter after the Supreme Court issued comprehensive directions.
material_facts: The Supreme Court had monitored the matter for almost five years and issued comprehensive directions to address pollution, compensation, restoration, and industrial controls.
The Court considered that the Madras High Court would be better placed to monitor the matter and other environmental cases thereafter.
issues.conclusion: The matter was transferred to the High Court to be dealt with under Article 226 and in accordance with the Supreme Court’s directions; the High Court could issue appropriate further orders.
issues.legal_principle: The Court exercised its powers in the proceeding under Article 32 of the Constitution and directed that the matter continue before the High Court under Article 226. It left the High Court free to make appropriate orders consistent with the directions already issued.

predicates.environmental_public_interest_proceeding: The proceeding concerns public interests affected by environmental conditions.
predicates.supreme_court_has_issued_comprehensive_d: The Supreme Court has issued comprehensive directions addressing the matter.
predicates.continuing_local_monitoring_is_needed: Further monitoring of compliance and developments remains necessary.

issues.definition: When an environmental public-interest proceeding requires continued local monitoring after comprehensive Supreme Court directions, the High Court should continue monitoring consistently with those directions.
